goals: Describe an eigenvector as a direction that only gets stretched
Connect eigenvectors of a covariance matrix to PCA
Interpret eigenvalues as "how much variance" lies along a direction
why: Eigenvectors are the engine of PCA, Google's original PageRank, and spectral clustering. Whenever you hear "principal components", eigenvectors are underneath.
explain: A matrix transforms vectors: it rotates, stretches or squashes them. Most vectors change direction. A few special directions only get **stretched or shrunk, never turned**. Those are the **eigenvectors**.
The amount of stretching is the **eigenvalue**. Eigenvalue 3 means "this direction gets three times longer"; 0.5 means it is halved.

In data science the key matrix is the **covariance matrix** of your features. Its eigenvectors point along the directions where the data spreads out most, and the eigenvalues say how much spread (variance) there is in each direction.
PCA keeps the eigenvectors with the largest eigenvalues and drops the rest. That compresses 50 correlated features into, say, 5 directions that hold most of the information.

formula.plain: Applying matrix A to eigenvector v gives the same direction v, just scaled by the number λ (the eigenvalue).

example.title: Spotting eigenvectors by testing arrows
steps: A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]]. Multiply three arrows by A and see which ones stay on their own line.
A [1, 0] = [2, 1]: the arrow pointed east, now north-east. Turned, so not an eigenvector.
A [1, 1] = [3, 3] = 3 × [1, 1]: same direction, three times longer. Eigenvector, eigenvalue λ = 3.
example.result: A stretches the diagonal direction by 3 and leaves the anti-diagonal alone; every other arrow gets pulled towards the diagonal. If A were a covariance matrix, the [1, 1] direction would hold 3 / (3 + 1) = 75% of the variance, and PCA would keep it first.

mistakes: Forgetting to scale features before PCA: a feature with big units dominates the covariance matrix.
Thinking eigenvectors are features. They are new directions made from combinations of the original features.
takeaways: Eigenvector = direction that is only stretched
Eigenvalue = how much it is stretched (variance along it, for a covariance matrix)

check.q: An eigenvalue of 0 means the direction…
options: Is squashed to nothing (no variance along it)
check.why: λ = 0 collapses that direction. For a covariance matrix, there is no spread along it.

check.q: Eigenvalues are 6, 3 and 1. What share of variance does the first component hold?

practice.code:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2, 1], [1, 2]])
vals, vecs = np.linalg.eigh(A)    # symmetric matrix → eigh
print(vals)                       # [1. 3.]
print(vecs)                       # columns ∝ [1, −1] and [1, 1]
print(A @ np.array([1, 1]))       # [3 3] = 3 × [1, 1]
print(vals / vals.sum())          # [0.25 0.75] share of 'variance' per direction
